KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry with fall-like temperatures today and
tonight. 

A cooler airmass settles over the region early this morning 
resulting a cool start to the day today with temperatures in the 40s 
and 50s this morning. Expect dry conditions today with surface high 
pressure in place. The cooler airmass stays put with 850mb 
temperatures 6-9C. This will support fall-like temperatures in the 
mid 60s for most, flirting with 70 in the CT Valley. Northeast flow 
with likely keep the immediate eastern coastal areas cooler in the 
low 60s. Tonight, high pressure begins to shift offshore as our next 
system approaches from the west. With cloud cover not increasing 
until sunrise, there should be enough of a window with clear skies 
and light winds to support efficient cooling tonight. Temperatures 
likely fall into the 40s for a good part of southern New England. CT 
and RI may end up a little warmer as WAA begins to push in after 
2AM which would limit their window of cooling. 

The extended period of NE winds will help develop a swell with 
longer wave periods across the eastern waters for today. This will 
increase the risk for rip currents for the east-facing beaches 
including Nantucket today. If you plan on heading to the beach 
despite the cooler temperatures, please use caution. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Rain likely Sunday into Monday, although there 
still remains uncertainty in the exact amounts. Showers may 
linger through early next week. A coastal system is possible 
late week. 

Model guidance continues to stay in general agreement to support 
rainfall Sunday into Monday. A shortwave approaches from the 
northwest coupled with an 850mb jet positioning over southern New 
England allow advection of moisture from the south and increased 
lift. PWATS increase to 1.2-1.8", around 160-180 percent of normal. 
A low pressure system tracks east from the Great Lakes region Sunday 
putting southern New England in the warm sector as its warm front 
shifts northward. With its cold front trailing from the west, this 
should provide sufficient convergence for widespread rainfall. Model 
guidance has consistently been indicating lacking instability with 
this system which would likely limit the rain rates and thus limit 
the threat for heavy rain and flash flooding. There is still some 
spread in expected totals liking owing to track differences, 
but ensembles show a more likely range of a few tenths to around
1 inch. Some solutions such as the ECMWF/ensemble indicate 
potential for greater than 1.0" with ensemble probabilities of 
20-50% along the east slope of the Berkshires. Other solutions 
lean lighter with amounts 0.25-0.50". 3 and 6 hour QPF doesn't 
approach FFG, but some pockets of moderate or very brief heavy 
rain are possible. In terms of timing, rain likely spreads from 
west to east Sunday morning with widespread rain arriving by the
afternoon. Rain continues overnight into Monday. 

How long the rain lingers Monday will depend on how progressive the 
system/front is. There are difference across guidance in the speed 
which has led to some uncertainty in how long showers linger around 
on Monday. If showers were to linger, it would more likely effect 
areas more south and east (Cape/Islands or south coast). Fall-like 
temperatures are likely behind the front on Monday with breezy 
northerly winds. There is potential for another system to brush 
southern New England Tuesday bringing showers; however, this is 
lower probability as there lacking agreement with how north this 
system tracks at this time. 

There is good agreement across model guidance with a fairly strong 
surface high shifting over Quebec Tuesday into mid-week. This will 
keep a cooler than normal airmass over the northeast supporting cool 
more fall-like temperatures continuing through the week. 
Deterministic and ensemble guidance continues to hint at the 
potential for a coastal low pressure system sometime Thursday into 
Friday. However, there is still a fair amount of uncertainty in the 
details of the pattern that will influence the track of this low. 
Some solutions feature a low track closer to southern New England 
while others well off shore. Pretty low confidence at point, but 
warrants monitoring as it would bring potential for stronger winds, 
rough seas for the coastal waters and potentially another round of 
rainfall.
